S6 Looking ahead: future LTSSL methods

While DeCon has achieved outstanding performance, we have observed that recent popular foundation models [63] can achieve excellent performance on downstream tasks through fine-tuning [64, 65, 66, 67]. Therefore, we investigate whether fine-tuning foundation models can further enhance the performance of the LTSSL method. We choose CLIP [63] for fine-tuning due to its strong generalization ability. CLIP is a multimodal model to align images and text in a shared embedding space, facilitating tasks like image classification, generation, and zero-shot learning across various domains [65]. When considering full fine-tuning the model, the target tasks often require a substantial amount of data for effective adaptation [68, 69]. However, for LTSSL tasks, labeled data are scarce and severely imbalanced, hindering full fine-tuning from achieving satisfactory performance. Therefore, motivated by [65], we attempt to leverage the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy [61, 62, 70] for fine-tuning to enhance the generalization performance of LTSSL models. PEFT strategies typically freeze the pre-trained model while introducing a few learnable parameters for adaptation. The results are shown in Table S6, and we utilize Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) [61] and AdaptFormer [62] for fine-tuning. VPT prepends learnable prompts optimized during the training at each transformer layer. AdaptFormer adds a bottleneck module, which is parallel to the FFN layer. The incorporation of VPT and AdaptFormer facilitates a notable 17.6% and 18.2% performance improvement for DeCon compared to the Wide ResNet-based model [52]. Additionally, we find that DeCon outperforms ACR by 0.6% when employing PEFT on CIFAR-10-LT and CIFAR-100-LT, further demonstrating the broad applicability of DeCon. Regarding the STL10-LT, we observe that the performance of all methods has almost saturated, with error rates generally below 2%. We advocate PEFT as a promising direction for LTSSL with foundation models in the future.

Next, we further clarify the relationship between DeCon and CLIP, as well as practical challenges in this setting.

Complementarity between CLIP and DeCon

CLIP provides strong pre-trained representations that can improve feature quality, but it does not inherently solve classifier bias caused by long-tailed labeled data in the target task.

  • •

    Representation vs. decision boundary: CLIP mainly improves the feature space (representation learning). However, when fine-tuned (including via PEFT) on a highly imbalanced labeled set, the resulting decision boundaries can still skew towards head classes. DeCon addresses this issue at the objective/optimization level through cross-branch interactions and distribution-aware correction.

  • •

    Empirical evidence: As shown in Table S6, applying DeCon on top of CLIP (via VPT or AdaptFormer) yields consistent improvements (e.g., surpassing ACR by 0.6% and FixMatch by 1.9%). This suggests that DeCon remains beneficial even with strong foundation-model representations.

Practical challenges when using CLIP for LTSSL

Integrating foundation models into LTSSL is non-trivial and faces several challenges beyond standard fine-tuning:

  • •

    Biased adaptation with scarce, imbalanced labels: Adapting a generic model to a specific task with extremely scarce and long-tailed labeled data can quickly introduce bias towards head classes.

  • •

    Noisy pseudo-labeling under imbalance: In SSL, the model generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled data. If adaptation is biased, pseudo-labels can be skewed and reinforce the imbalance. A key challenge is how to leverage unlabeled data—with an unknown class prior—to regularize adaptation, which is aligned with the motivation of DeCon’s dual-branch interaction.

S7 Theoretical Analysis for DeCon

S7.1 Setup and Notation

We consider a labeled set 𝒟l={(xi(l),yi(l))}i=1N\mathcal{D}^{l}=\{(x^{(l)}_{i},y^{(l)}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} and an unlabeled set 𝒟u={xj(u)}j=1M\mathcal{D}^{u}=\{x^{(u)}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} with CC classes. Let πl∈ΔC−1\pi_{l}\in\Delta^{C-1} be the labeled class prior and πu∈ΔC−1\pi_{u}\in\Delta^{C-1} be the (unknown) unlabeled/test prior. We write [C]:={1,2,…,C}[C]:=\{1,2,\ldots,C\} and ΔC−1\Delta^{C-1} for the probability simplex.

Two branches and two EMA priors

Let ftf_{t} denote standard-branch logits and f~t\tilde{f}_{t} denote balanced-branch logits at step tt. The method maintains two EMA priors: (i) π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t} estimated from the balanced branch (used in decoupled distribution alignment, Eq. (4) in the main text); (ii) πts\pi^{s}_{t} estimated from the standard branch (used in pseudo-label correction, Eq. (7) in the main text). Let δ⁡(⋅)\delta(\cdot) be the softmax, so δ⁡(z)∈int⁡(ΔC−1)\delta(z)\in\mathrm{int}(\Delta^{C-1}) for any finite logits zz.

Temperatures

τ2>0\tau_{2}>0 is the scale used in standard-branch decoupled distribution alignment (Eq. (4)). τ1>0\tau_{1}>0 is the scale used in pseudo-label correction (Eq. (7)). τ3>0\tau_{3}>0 is the post-hoc adjustment scale used at inference (Eq. (11)).

Assumption 1 (Label shift).

There exists a shared class-conditional distribution p⁡(x∣y)p(x\mid y) such that pl​(x,y)=πl​(y)​p​(x∣y)p_{l}(x,y)=\pi_{l}(y)p(x\mid y) and pu​(x,y)=πu​(y)​p​(x∣y)p_{u}(x,y)=\pi_{u}(y)p(x\mid y).

Positivity for log terms

All priors used inside log⁡(⋅)\log(\cdot) are strictly positive. Softmax outputs are strictly positive; EMA priors remain in the simplex interior by convexity. Implementations may clip probabilities for numerical stability.

S7.2 Decouple: Balanced Softmax Recovers Class-Conditional Scores in an Idealized Limit

For any prior π∈ΔC−1\pi\in\Delta^{C-1} define the prior-weighted predictive distribution

pf~π​(y∣x):=exp⁡(f~y​(x))​π​(y)∑c=1Cexp⁡(f~c​(x))​π​(c).p_{\tilde{f}}^{\pi}(y\mid x):=\frac{\exp(\tilde{f}_{y}(x))\pi(y)}{\sum_{c=1}^{C}\exp(\tilde{f}_{c}(x))\pi(c)}.
Proposition 1 (Labeled-only decoupling property).

Assume Assumption 1 and realizability: there exists f~\tilde{f} such that pf~πl(⋅∣x)=pl(⋅∣x)p_{\tilde{f}}^{\pi_{l}}(\cdot\mid x)=p_{l}(\cdot\mid x) almost surely. Then any population minimizer f~⋆\tilde{f}^{\star} of 𝔼(x,y)∼pl​[−log⁡pf~πl​(y∣x)]\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim p_{l}}\big[-\log p_{\tilde{f}}^{\pi_{l}}(y\mid x)\big] satisfies

f~y⋆​(x)=log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+b⁡(x),\tilde{f}^{\star}_{y}(x)=\log p(x\mid y)+b(x),

for some measurable b⁡(x)b(x) independent of yy.

Proposition 2 (Decoupled scores imply prior-adaptable Bayes prediction).

Assume Assumption 1. Fix any target prior πtar∈ΔC−1\pi_{\mathrm{tar}}\in\Delta^{C-1}. If a model f~\tilde{f} satisfies f~y​(x)=log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+b⁡(x)\tilde{f}_{y}(x)=\log p(x\mid y)+b(x) for some b⁡(x)b(x) independent of yy, then

arg⁡maxy∈[C]​{f~y​(x)+log⁡πtar​(y)}=arg⁡maxy∈[C]​{log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+log⁡πtar​(y)},\arg\max_{y\in[C]}\{\tilde{f}_{y}(x)+\log\pi_{\mathrm{tar}}(y)\}=\arg\max_{y\in[C]}\{\log p(x\mid y)+\log\pi_{\mathrm{tar}}(y)\},

which is Bayes-optimal under label shift with target prior πtar\pi_{\mathrm{tar}}.

S7.3 EMA Prior Estimators: Deterministic Dynamics (Mean-Field) and Bounded Variation

Mean-field vs. mini-batch.

In the implementation, priors are updated using mini-batch averages. For a careful and non-misleading convergence statement, we analyze the mean-field (population) update:

p¯t:=𝔼x∼pu​[δ⁡(st​(x))]∈ΔC−1,\bar{p}_{t}:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{u}}\big[\delta(s_{t}(x))\big]\in\Delta^{C-1},

where sts_{t} is either ftf_{t} (for πts\pi^{s}_{t}) or f~t\tilde{f}_{t} (for π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t}). Mini-batch updates are unbiased estimators of p¯t\bar{p}_{t} and EMA smoothing controls their variance; we do not claim almost-sure pointwise convergence for the stochastic EMA with persistent sampling noise.

Generic EMA recursion.

Let πt\pi_{t} denote any EMA prior updated by

πt+1=m​πt+(1−m)​p¯t,m∈(0,1).\pi_{t+1}=m\pi_{t}+(1-m)\bar{p}_{t},\qquad m\in(0,1). (S1)
Lemma 1 (Closed form and bounded step size).

The EMA recursion (S1) admits the closed form

πt=mt​π0+(1−m)​∑k=0t−1mt−1−k​p¯k.\pi_{t}=m^{t}\pi_{0}+(1-m)\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}m^{t-1-k}\bar{p}_{k}.

Moreover,

‖πt+1−πt‖1=(1−m)​‖p¯t−πt‖1≤2​(1−m).\|\pi_{t+1}-\pi_{t}\|_{1}=(1-m)\|\bar{p}_{t}-\pi_{t}\|_{1}\leq 2(1-m).
Lemma 2 (Tracking bound and convergence under convergent drive).

Define et:=πt−p¯te_{t}:=\pi_{t}-\bar{p}_{t}. Then for all t≥1t\geq 1,

‖et‖1≤mt​‖e0‖1+∑k=1tmt−k​‖p¯k−p¯k−1‖1.\|e_{t}\|_{1}\leq m^{t}\|e_{0}\|_{1}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}m^{t-k}\|\bar{p}_{k}-\bar{p}_{k-1}\|_{1}. (S2)

In particular, if p¯t→p¯∞\bar{p}_{t}\to\bar{p}_{\infty}, then πt→p¯∞\pi_{t}\to\bar{p}_{\infty}.

S7.4 What Prediction-Based Prior Estimation Can (and Cannot) Guarantee

Balanced-branch prediction marginal

Define

πtpred:=𝔼x∼pu​[δ⁡(f~t​(x))]∈ΔC−1,π^t:=1M​∑j=1Mδ⁡(f~t​(xj(u))).\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{u}}\big[\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x))\big]\in\Delta^{C-1},\qquad\hat{\pi}_{t}:=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x^{(u)}_{j})).
Theorem 1 (Error decomposition for prediction-marginal estimation).

Fix tt and treat f~t\tilde{f}_{t} as fixed. With probability at least 1−ν1-\nu over 𝒟u\mathcal{D}^{u} (i.i.d. from pu​(x)p_{u}(x)),

‖π^t−πu‖1≤‖πtpred−πu‖1⏟model-induced bias+2​CM+2​log⁡(1/ν)M.\|\hat{\pi}_{t}-\pi_{u}\|_{1}\leq\underbrace{\|\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}-\pi_{u}\|_{1}}_{\text{model-induced bias}}+2\sqrt{\frac{C}{M}}+\sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\nu)}{M}}.

Moreover,

∥πtpred−πu∥1≤𝔼x∼pu∥δ(f~t(x))−pu(⋅∣x)∥1.\|\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}-\pi_{u}\|_{1}\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{u}}\big\|\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x))-p_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\big\|_{1}.

Key takeaway

Theorem 1 does not claim that π^t\hat{\pi}_{t} is close to πu\pi_{u}. It cleanly separates two effects: sampling noise (controlled by MM) and model-induced bias (depends on prediction quality). No prediction-only estimator can generally avoid this dependence. Therefore, our algorithmic justification does not rely on assuming π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t} or πts\pi^{s}_{t} is a universally consistent estimator of πu\pi_{u}.

Proposition 3 (Uniform-prior posterior effect).

Assume f~\tilde{f} satisfies the labeled-only decoupling form in Proposition 1. Then

δ​(f~​(x))y=p⁡(x∣y)∑c=1Cp⁡(x∣c)=:punif​(y∣x),\delta(\tilde{f}(x))_{y}=\frac{p(x\mid y)}{\sum_{c=1}^{C}p(x\mid c)}=:p^{\mathrm{unif}}(y\mid x),

i.e., the posterior induced by a uniform class prior. Consequently, in the large-sample limit, π^\hat{\pi} converges to

πunif:=𝔼x∼pu[punif(⋅∣x)],\pi^{\mathrm{unif}}:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{u}}\big[p^{\mathrm{unif}}(\cdot\mid x)\big],

which may differ from πu\pi_{u} when classes overlap.

Why Proposition 3 is not a contradiction to DeCon

Proposition 3 shows only that a perfectly decoupled model produces a uniform-prior posterior. It does not imply that the induced marginal πunif\pi^{\mathrm{unif}} must be the uniform vector, nor does it invalidate the algorithm, because DeCon does not require π~t=πu\tilde{\pi}_{t}=\pi_{u} to be exact. Instead, DeCon uses prior signals through (i) margin-robust logit adjustments, and (ii) a self-paced importance weight that suppresses DA/PLC-sensitive pseudo-labels.

S7.5 Pseudo-Label Correction (PLC) and Self-Paced Importance Weighting (Eq. (7–9) in Main Text)

PLC distribution.

Let ptpre(⋅∣x):=δ(ft(x))p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x):=\delta(f_{t}(x)) and define

ptplc​(y∣x)=ptpre​(y∣x)⋅(πts​(y))−τ1∑c=1Cptpre​(c∣x)⋅(πts​(c))−τ1.p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(y\mid x)=\frac{p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(y\mid x)\cdot\big(\pi^{s}_{t}(y)\big)^{-\tau_{1}}}{\sum_{c=1}^{C}p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(c\mid x)\cdot\big(\pi^{s}_{t}(c)\big)^{-\tau_{1}}}. (S3)

The pseudo-label used to supervise the balanced branch is q^tplc​(x):=arg⁡maxy​ptplc​(y∣x)\hat{q}^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(x):=\arg\max_{y}p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(y\mid x), matching Eq. (7).

Lemma 3 (Logit form of PLC).

q^tplc​(x)\hat{q}^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(x) is equivalently

q^tplc​(x)=arg⁡maxy∈[C]​{log⁡ptpre​(y∣x)−τ1​log⁡πts​(y)}.\hat{q}^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(x)=\arg\max_{y\in[C]}\Big\{\log p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(y\mid x)-\tau_{1}\log\pi^{s}_{t}(y)\Big\}.

Overlap score and weight (implementation-aligned).

Define

αpre​(x):=maxc⁡ptpre​(c∣x),αplc​(x):=maxc⁡ptplc​(c∣x),ηt​(x):=maxc⁡ptpre​(c∣x)​ptplc​(c∣x)∈[0,1].\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x):=\max_{c}p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(c\mid x),\quad\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x):=\max_{c}p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(c\mid x),\quad\eta_{t}(x):=\max_{c}\,p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(c\mid x)\,p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(c\mid x)\in[0,1].

The implementation uses ψt​(x)=γt​ηt​(x)\psi_{t}(x)=\gamma_{t}\eta_{t}(x) (Eq. (8–9)) for a global scalar γt\gamma_{t}.

Lemma 4 (Self-paced gating property of η\eta (no accuracy assumption)).

For any xx,

ηt​(x)≤αpre​(x)​αplc​(x).\eta_{t}(x)\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x)\,\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x).

If moreover the maximizer class agrees (i.e., argmaxptpre(⋅∣x)=argmaxptplc(⋅∣x)\arg\max p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x)=\arg\max p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x)) and is unique, then

ηt​(x)=αpre​(x)​αplc​(x).\eta_{t}(x)=\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x)\,\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x).

Consequently, large ηt​(x)\eta_{t}(x) is only possible when both (i) both distributions are confident and (ii) they agree on the top class.

Lemma 5 (Disagreement implies small overlap).

If argmaxptpre(⋅∣x)≠argmaxptplc(⋅∣x)\arg\max p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x)\neq\arg\max p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x), then

ηt​(x)≤1−min⁡{αpre​(x),αplc​(x)}.\eta_{t}(x)\leq 1-\min\{\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x),\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x)\}.

How DeCon avoids “early inaccurate prior” harm

Lemma 4 is the crucial non-circular mechanism statement: even if πts\pi^{s}_{t} is inaccurate early (hence PLC is noisy), the unlabeled term is automatically suppressed when the model is uncertain (small αpre,αplc\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}},\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}), and also suppressed when PLC flips labels (Lemma 5). Thus the balanced branch is not forced to learn from unstable pseudo-labels at the beginning; the interaction ramps up only as the standard branch becomes confident, breaking the “you must already be accurate” loop.

S7.6 Decoupled Distribution Alignment (DDA) on Standard Branch (Eq. (4)) and Margin Robustness

Let ptstd(⋅∣x):=δ(ft(x))p^{\mathrm{std}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x):=\delta(f_{t}(x)). DDA uses π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t} to form

ptdda​(y∣x)=ptstd​(y∣x)⋅(πl​(y)π~t​(y))τ2∑c=1Cptstd​(c∣x)⋅(πl​(c)π~t​(c))τ2.p^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(y\mid x)=\frac{p^{\mathrm{std}}_{t}(y\mid x)\cdot\left(\frac{\pi_{l}(y)}{\tilde{\pi}_{t}(y)}\right)^{\tau_{2}}}{\sum_{c=1}^{C}p^{\mathrm{std}}_{t}(c\mid x)\cdot\left(\frac{\pi_{l}(c)}{\tilde{\pi}_{t}(c)}\right)^{\tau_{2}}}. (S4)

So the logit form of DDA is:

arg⁡maxy∈[C]​ptdda​(y∣x)=arg⁡maxy∈[C]​{log⁡ptstd​(y∣x)+τ2​(log⁡πl​(y)−log⁡π~t​(y))}.\arg\max_{y\in[C]}p^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(y\mid x)=\arg\max_{y\in[C]}\Big\{\log p^{\mathrm{std}}_{t}(y\mid x)+\tau_{2}\big(\log\pi_{l}(y)-\log\tilde{\pi}_{t}(y)\big)\Big\}. (S5)
Lemma 6 (Argmax robustness to log-prior perturbation).

Define δt(e):=‖log⁡π~t−log⁡πu‖∞\delta_{t}^{(e)}:=\|\log\tilde{\pi}_{t}-\log\pi_{u}\|_{\infty} and

stdda​(y∣x;π):=log⁡ptstd​(y∣x)+τ2​(log⁡πl​(y)−log⁡π⁡(y)).s^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(y\mid x;\pi):=\log p^{\mathrm{std}}_{t}(y\mid x)+\tau_{2}\big(\log\pi_{l}(y)-\log\pi(y)\big).

Let y⋆​(x,πu)y^{\star}(x;\pi_{u}) be the argmax and define the margin

Δtdda​(x,πu):=stdda​(y⋆​(x,πu)∣x;πu)−maxy≠y⋆​(x,πu)⁡stdda​(y∣x;πu).\Delta^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(x;\pi_{u}):=s^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}\big(y^{\star}(x;\pi_{u})\mid x;\pi_{u}\big)-\max_{y\neq y^{\star}(x;\pi_{u})}s^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(y\mid x;\pi_{u}).

If Δtdda​(x,πu)>2​τ2​δt(e)\Delta^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(x;\pi_{u})>2\tau_{2}\delta_{t}^{(e)}, then the argmax under π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t} equals that under πu\pi_{u}.

Remark

Lemma 6 is a conservative robustness statement (prevents catastrophic flips on high-margin points). We do not claim it proves performance gain by itself.

S7.7 Eventual Stationarity Without Circular “Assume Convergence”

We now give a non-circular stationarity theorem. Instead of assuming the scores converge, we use a standard optimization-tail condition that implies the logits (and hence the coupling signals) are Cauchy.

Lemma 7 (Cauchy logits under summable step sizes (one sufficient condition)).

Let θt\theta_{t} be parameters of a branch and hθ​(x)∈ℝCh_{\theta}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{C} its logits (either ff or f~\tilde{f}). Assume: (i) the update satisfies θt+1=θt−αt​gt\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\alpha_{t}g_{t} with ‖gt‖2≤G\|g_{t}\|_{2}\leq G almost surely; (ii) ∑t=0∞αt<∞\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_{t}<\infty; (iii) hθ​(x)h_{\theta}(x) is LL-Lipschitz in parameters: ‖hθ​(x)−hθ′​(x)‖∞≤L​‖θ−θ′‖2\|h_{\theta}(x)-h_{\theta^{\prime}}(x)\|_{\infty}\leq L\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2}. Then for every xx,

∑t=0∞‖hθt+1​(x)−hθt​(x)‖∞<∞,\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\|h_{\theta_{t+1}}(x)-h_{\theta_{t}}(x)\|_{\infty}<\infty,

hence hθt​(x)h_{\theta_{t}}(x) converges (Cauchy) as t→∞t\to\infty.

Theorem 2 (Eventual stationarity of PLC pseudo-labels and overlap weights (mean-field)).

Assume the mean-field EMA prior updates (S1) for both π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t} and πts\pi^{s}_{t}, with p¯t\bar{p}_{t} defined as population prediction marginals. Assume furthermore that both branches satisfy the conditions of Lemma 7 (so ft​(x)f_{t}(x) and f~t​(x)\tilde{f}_{t}(x) converge pointwise), and that for almost every xx, the limiting PLC score vector

u∞​(y∣x):=limt→∞(log⁡δ​(ft​(x))y−τ1​log⁡πts​(y))u_{\infty}(y\mid x):=\lim_{t\to\infty}\Big(\log\delta(f_{t}(x))_{y}-\tau_{1}\log\pi^{s}_{t}(y)\Big)

has a unique maximizer (no ties). Then for almost every xx:

  1. 1.

    (PLC pseudo-label stabilization) There exists T⁡(x)T(x) such that for all t≥T⁡(x)t\geq T(x), q^tplc​(x)\hat{q}^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(x) is constant.

  2. 2.

    (Prior stabilization) The EMA priors π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t} and πts\pi^{s}_{t} converge in ℓ1\ell_{1}.

  3. 3.

    (Overlap/weight stabilization) ηt​(x)\eta_{t}(x) converges. If γt→γ∞<∞\gamma_{t}\to\gamma_{\infty}<\infty, then ψt​(x)=γt​ηt​(x)\psi_{t}(x)=\gamma_{t}\eta_{t}(x) converges.

What this theorem does and does not claim

Theorem 2 proves a stationarity property of the coupled discrete/continuous signals under a standard “optimization tail” condition. It does not claim convergence to a globally optimal classifier, nor that the stationary point is correct.

S7.8 Post-hoc Adjustment (Eq. (11)) and Robustness

At inference,

q^(b)​(x)=arg⁡maxy​{f~t​(x)y−τ3​log⁡π~t​(y)}.\hat{q}^{(b)}(x)=\arg\max_{y}\{\tilde{f}_{t}(x)_{y}-\tau_{3}\log\tilde{\pi}_{t}(y)\}.
Lemma 8 (Probability form of post-hoc adjustment).

Let pt​(y∣x)=δ​(f~t​(x))yp_{t}(y\mid x)=\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x))_{y} and ptadj​(y∣x)=δ​(f~t​(x)−τ3​log⁡π~t)yp_{t}^{\mathrm{adj}}(y\mid x)=\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x)-\tau_{3}\log\tilde{\pi}_{t})_{y}. Then

ptadj​(y∣x)=pt​(y∣x)⋅π~t​(y)−τ3∑c=1Cpt​(c∣x)⋅π~t​(c)−τ3.p_{t}^{\mathrm{adj}}(y\mid x)=\frac{p_{t}(y\mid x)\cdot\tilde{\pi}_{t}(y)^{-\tau_{3}}}{\sum_{c=1}^{C}p_{t}(c\mid x)\cdot\tilde{\pi}_{t}(c)^{-\tau_{3}}}.
Lemma 9 (Post-hoc argmax robustness to prior error).

Fix xx and define scores

rt​(y∣x;π):=f~t​(x)y−τ3​log⁡π⁡(y).r_{t}(y\mid x;\pi):=\tilde{f}_{t}(x)_{y}-\tau_{3}\log\pi(y).

Let y⋆​(x,πu)=arg⁡maxy​rt​(y∣x;πu)y^{\star}(x;\pi_{u})=\arg\max_{y}r_{t}(y\mid x;\pi_{u}) and define the margin

Γt​(x,πu):=rt​(y⋆​(x,πu)∣x;πu)−maxy≠y⋆​(x,πu)⁡rt​(y∣x;πu).\Gamma_{t}(x;\pi_{u}):=r_{t}\big(y^{\star}(x;\pi_{u})\mid x;\pi_{u}\big)-\max_{y\neq y^{\star}(x;\pi_{u})}r_{t}(y\mid x;\pi_{u}).

If Γt​(x,πu)>2​τ3​‖log⁡π~t−log⁡πu‖∞\Gamma_{t}(x;\pi_{u})>2\tau_{3}\|\log\tilde{\pi}_{t}-\log\pi_{u}\|_{\infty}, then

arg⁡maxy​rt​(y∣x;π~t)=arg⁡maxy​rt​(y∣x;πu).\arg\max_{y}r_{t}(y\mid x;\tilde{\pi}_{t})=\arg\max_{y}r_{t}(y\mid x;\pi_{u}).

S8 Proofs

S8.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

At a realizable population optimum, pf~⋆πl(⋅∣x)=pl(⋅∣x)p_{\tilde{f}^{\star}}^{\pi_{l}}(\cdot\mid x)=p_{l}(\cdot\mid x) almost surely. Thus for each x,yx,y,

exp⁡(f~y⋆​(x))​πl​(y)∑cexp⁡(f~c⋆​(x))​πl​(c)=πl​(y)​p​(x∣y)∑cπl​(c)​p​(x∣c).\frac{\exp(\tilde{f}^{\star}_{y}(x))\pi_{l}(y)}{\sum_{c}\exp(\tilde{f}^{\star}_{c}(x))\pi_{l}(c)}=\frac{\pi_{l}(y)p(x\mid y)}{\sum_{c}\pi_{l}(c)p(x\mid c)}.

Cancel πl​(y)\pi_{l}(y) to obtain exp⁡(f~y⋆​(x))=A⁡(x)​p​(x∣y)\exp(\tilde{f}^{\star}_{y}(x))=A(x)p(x\mid y) for some A⁡(x)>0A(x)>0 independent of yy, hence f~y⋆​(x)=log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+b⁡(x)\tilde{f}^{\star}_{y}(x)=\log p(x\mid y)+b(x) where b⁡(x):=log⁡A⁡(x)b(x):=\log A(x). ∎

S8.2 Proof of Proposition 2

Proof.

If f~y​(x)=log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+b⁡(x)\tilde{f}_{y}(x)=\log p(x\mid y)+b(x) with b⁡(x)b(x) independent of yy, then for any πtar\pi_{\mathrm{tar}},

arg⁡maxy​{f~y​(x)+log⁡πtar​(y)}=arg⁡maxy​{log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+log⁡πtar​(y)},\arg\max_{y}\{\tilde{f}_{y}(x)+\log\pi_{\mathrm{tar}}(y)\}=\arg\max_{y}\{\log p(x\mid y)+\log\pi_{\mathrm{tar}}(y)\},

since adding b⁡(x)b(x) does not change the argmax over yy. Under label shift, the right-hand side is the Bayes rule for target prior πtar\pi_{\mathrm{tar}}. ∎

S8.3 Proof of Lemma 1

Proof.

Unroll πt+1=m​πt+(1−m)​p¯t\pi_{t+1}=m\pi_{t}+(1-m)\bar{p}_{t} to obtain the closed form. For the step bound,

‖πt+1−πt‖1=(1−m)​‖p¯t−πt‖1≤2​(1−m),\|\pi_{t+1}-\pi_{t}\|_{1}=(1-m)\|\bar{p}_{t}-\pi_{t}\|_{1}\leq 2(1-m),

since any two simplex vectors differ by at most 22 in ℓ1\ell_{1}. ∎

S8.4 Proof of Lemma 2

Proof.

Define et:=πt−p¯te_{t}:=\pi_{t}-\bar{p}_{t}. Then

et+1=πt+1−p¯t+1=m​πt+(1−m)​p¯t−p¯t+1=m⁡(πt−p¯t)+(p¯t−p¯t+1)=m​et+(p¯t−p¯t+1).e_{t+1}=\pi_{t+1}-\bar{p}_{t+1}=m\pi_{t}+(1-m)\bar{p}_{t}-\bar{p}_{t+1}=m(\pi_{t}-\bar{p}_{t})+(\bar{p}_{t}-\bar{p}_{t+1})=me_{t}+(\bar{p}_{t}-\bar{p}_{t+1}).

Iterating,

et=mt​e0+∑k=1tmt−k​(p¯k−1−p¯k),e_{t}=m^{t}e_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}m^{t-k}(\bar{p}_{k-1}-\bar{p}_{k}),

hence (S2) by triangle inequality. If p¯t→p¯∞\bar{p}_{t}\to\bar{p}_{\infty}, then ‖p¯k−p¯k−1‖1→0\|\bar{p}_{k}-\bar{p}_{k-1}\|_{1}\to 0 and the convolution with mt−km^{t-k} vanishes, so πt−p¯t=et→0\pi_{t}-\bar{p}_{t}=e_{t}\to 0 and thus πt→p¯∞\pi_{t}\to\bar{p}_{\infty}. ∎

S8.5 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

Let Xj:=δ⁡(f~t​(xj(u)))∈ΔC−1X_{j}:=\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x^{(u)}_{j}))\in\Delta^{C-1}, and let μ:=𝔼⁡[Xj]=πtpred\mu:=\mathbb{E}[X_{j}]=\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}. Define μ^:=1M​∑j=1MXj=π^t\hat{\mu}:=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}X_{j}=\hat{\pi}_{t}.

Step 1 (McDiarmid). Consider F⁡(X1,…,XM):=‖1M​∑j=1MXj−μ‖1F(X_{1},\dots,X_{M}):=\big\|\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}X_{j}-\mu\big\|_{1}. Changing one sample changes the mean by at most 2M\frac{2}{M} in ℓ1\ell_{1}, so McDiarmid gives with probability at least 1−ν1-\nu,

‖μ^−μ‖1≤𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖1+2​log⁡(1/ν)M.\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{1}\leq\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{1}+\sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\nu)}{M}}.

𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖1≤2​𝔼​‖1M​∑j=1Mσj​Xj‖1,\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{1}\leq 2\,\mathbb{E}\Big\|\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sigma_{j}X_{j}\Big\|_{1},

with i.i.d. Rademacher σj\sigma_{j}. Conditioned on {Xj}\{X_{j}\}, by Khintchine, 𝔼σ​|∑jσj​Xj​(c)|≤∑jXj​(c)2\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\big|\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}X_{j}(c)\big|\leq\sqrt{\sum_{j}X_{j}(c)^{2}}. Thus

𝔼σ​‖∑jσj​Xj‖1≤∑c=1C∑j=1MXj​(c)2≤C​∑c=1C∑j=1MXj​(c)2.\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\Big\|\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}X_{j}\Big\|_{1}\leq\sum_{c=1}^{C}\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{M}X_{j}(c)^{2}}\leq\sqrt{C\sum_{c=1}^{C}\sum_{j=1}^{M}X_{j}(c)^{2}}.

Since Xj∈ΔC−1X_{j}\in\Delta^{C-1}, ∑cXj​(c)2≤1\sum_{c}X_{j}(c)^{2}\leq 1, so the last term is ≤C​M\leq\sqrt{CM}. Therefore 𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖1≤2​C/M\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{1}\leq 2\sqrt{C/M}. Combine with Step 1 and then triangle inequality ‖π^t−πu‖1≤‖πtpred−πu‖1+‖π^t−πtpred‖1\|\hat{\pi}_{t}-\pi_{u}\|_{1}\leq\|\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}-\pi_{u}\|_{1}+\|\hat{\pi}_{t}-\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}\|_{1}.

For the second claim, since πu=𝔼[pu(⋅∣x)]\pi_{u}=\mathbb{E}[p_{u}(\cdot\mid x)],

∥πtpred−πu∥1=∥𝔼[δ(f~t(x))−pu(⋅∣x)]∥1≤𝔼∥δ(f~t(x))−pu(⋅∣x)∥1\|\pi_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}-\pi_{u}\|_{1}=\Big\|\mathbb{E}\big[\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x))-p_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\big]\Big\|_{1}\leq\mathbb{E}\big\|\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x))-p_{u}(\cdot\mid x)\big\|_{1}

by Jensen. ∎

S8.6 Proof of Proposition 3

Proof.

If f~y​(x)=log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+b⁡(x)\tilde{f}_{y}(x)=\log p(x\mid y)+b(x), then

δ​(f~​(x))y=exp⁡(log⁡p⁡(x∣y)+b⁡(x))∑cexp⁡(log⁡p⁡(x∣c)+b⁡(x))=p⁡(x∣y)∑cp⁡(x∣c).\delta(\tilde{f}(x))_{y}=\frac{\exp(\log p(x\mid y)+b(x))}{\sum_{c}\exp(\log p(x\mid c)+b(x))}=\frac{p(x\mid y)}{\sum_{c}p(x\mid c)}.

Taking expectation over x∼pu​(x)x\sim p_{u}(x) gives πunif\pi^{\mathrm{unif}}. ∎

S8.7 Proof of Lemma 3

Proof.

From (S3), the unnormalized score is ptpre​(y∣x)​(πts​(y))−τ1p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(y\mid x)\,(\pi^{s}_{t}(y))^{-\tau_{1}}. Taking logs yields log⁡ptpre​(y∣x)−τ1​log⁡πts​(y)\log p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(y\mid x)-\tau_{1}\log\pi^{s}_{t}(y). The normalizer does not depend on yy, hence the argmax form. ∎

S8.8 Proof of Lemma 4

Proof.

For any cc, ptpre​(c∣x)≤αpre​(x)p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(c\mid x)\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x) and ptplc​(c∣x)≤αplc​(x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(c\mid x)\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x), hence ptpre​(c∣x)​ptplc​(c∣x)≤αpre​(x)​αplc​(x)p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(c\mid x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(c\mid x)\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x)\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x). Taking max over cc gives ηt​(x)≤αpre​(x)​αplc​(x)\eta_{t}(x)\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x)\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x).

If the unique maximizer agrees, say a=argmaxptpre(⋅∣x)=argmaxptplc(⋅∣x)a=\arg\max p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x)=\arg\max p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x), then ptpre​(a∣x)=αpre​(x)p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(a\mid x)=\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x) and ptplc​(a∣x)=αplc​(x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(a\mid x)=\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x), so ηt​(x)≥ptpre​(a∣x)​ptplc​(a∣x)=αpre​(x)​αplc​(x)\eta_{t}(x)\geq p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(a\mid x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(a\mid x)=\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x)\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x). Combine with the upper bound to get equality. ∎

S8.9 Proof of Lemma 5

Proof.

Let a:=argmaxptpre(⋅∣x)a:=\arg\max p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x) and b:=argmaxptplc(⋅∣x)b:=\arg\max p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x) with a≠ba\neq b. Then ptpre​(a∣x)=αpre​(x)p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(a\mid x)=\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x) and ptplc​(b∣x)=αplc​(x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(b\mid x)=\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x). Since a≠ba\neq b, ptplc​(a∣x)≤1−αplc​(x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(a\mid x)\leq 1-\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x), so

ptpre​(a∣x)​ptplc​(a∣x)≤αpre​(x)​(1−αplc​(x))≤1−αplc​(x).p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(a\mid x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(a\mid x)\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x)(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x))\leq 1-\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x).

Similarly ptpre​(b∣x)≤1−αpre​(x)p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(b\mid x)\leq 1-\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x), so

ptpre​(b∣x)​ptplc​(b∣x)≤(1−αpre​(x))​αplc​(x)≤1−αpre​(x).p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(b\mid x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(b\mid x)\leq(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x))\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x)\leq 1-\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x).

For any other c∉{a,b}c\notin\{a,b\}, both factors are ≤1−αpre​(x)\leq 1-\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x) and ≤1−αplc​(x)\leq 1-\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x), so the product is ≤(1−αpre​(x))​(1−αplc​(x))≤1−min⁡{αpre​(x),αplc​(x)}\leq(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x))(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x))\leq 1-\min\{\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}(x),\alpha_{\mathrm{plc}}(x)\}. Taking the maximum over cc yields the claim. ∎

S8.10 Proof of Lemma 6

Proof.

For any yy,

|stdda​(y∣x;π~t)−stdda​(y∣x;πu)|=τ2|log⁡π~t​(y)−log⁡πu​(y)|≤τ2​δt(e).|s^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(y\mid x;\tilde{\pi}_{t})-s^{\mathrm{dda}}_{t}(y\mid x;\pi_{u})|=\tau_{2}|\log\tilde{\pi}_{t}(y)-\log\pi_{u}(y)|\leq\tau_{2}\delta_{t}^{(e)}.

Thus both the top score and the best competing score can change by at most τ2​δt(e)\tau_{2}\delta_{t}^{(e)}, so the margin can shrink by at most 2​τ2​δt(e)2\tau_{2}\delta_{t}^{(e)}. If the margin remains larger, the ordering cannot change. ∎

S8.11 Proof of Lemma 7

Proof.

Since θt+1−θt=−αt​gt\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t}=-\alpha_{t}g_{t} and ‖gt‖2≤G\|g_{t}\|_{2}\leq G, we have ‖θt+1−θt‖2≤G​αt\|\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t}\|_{2}\leq G\alpha_{t}. By Lipschitzness,

‖hθt+1​(x)−hθt​(x)‖∞≤L​‖θt+1−θt‖2≤L​G​αt.\|h_{\theta_{t+1}}(x)-h_{\theta_{t}}(x)\|_{\infty}\leq L\|\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t}\|_{2}\leq LG\alpha_{t}.

Summing over tt gives ∑t‖hθt+1​(x)−hθt​(x)‖∞≤L​G​∑tαt<∞\sum_{t}\|h_{\theta_{t+1}}(x)-h_{\theta_{t}}(x)\|_{\infty}\leq LG\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}<\infty. Hence hθt​(x)h_{\theta_{t}}(x) is Cauchy and converges. ∎

S8.12 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

By Lemma 7, for every xx, ft​(x)→f∞​(x)f_{t}(x)\to f_{\infty}(x) and f~t​(x)→f~∞​(x)\tilde{f}_{t}(x)\to\tilde{f}_{\infty}(x). By continuity of softmax on ℝC\mathbb{R}^{C}, δ⁡(ft​(x))→δ⁡(f∞​(x))\delta(f_{t}(x))\to\delta(f_{\infty}(x)) pointwise. By dominated convergence (bounded in [0,1][0,1]), the population marginals p¯t=𝔼x∼pu​[δ⁡(ft​(x))]\bar{p}_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{u}}[\delta(f_{t}(x))] and similarly for f~t\tilde{f}_{t} converge. Then Lemma 2 implies πts\pi^{s}_{t} and π~t\tilde{\pi}_{t} converge.

Now log⁡δ​(ft​(x))y\log\delta(f_{t}(x))_{y} is continuous in ft​(x)f_{t}(x) whenever probabilities stay positive; this holds since logits converge to finite values and softmax outputs are in the simplex interior. Also log⁡πts​(y)\log\pi^{s}_{t}(y) converges since πts\pi^{s}_{t} converges in the interior. Therefore the PLC score vector ut​(y∣x)=log⁡δ​(ft​(x))y−τ1​log⁡πts​(y)u_{t}(y\mid x)=\log\delta(f_{t}(x))_{y}-\tau_{1}\log\pi^{s}_{t}(y) converges to u∞(⋅∣x)u_{\infty}(\cdot\mid x).

By the unique-maximizer assumption, there exists T⁡(x)T(x) such that for all t≥T⁡(x)t\geq T(x) the argmax of ut(⋅∣x)u_{t}(\cdot\mid x) equals that of u∞(⋅∣x)u_{\infty}(\cdot\mid x), hence q^tplc​(x)\hat{q}^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(x) is constant.

Finally, ptpre(⋅∣x)=δ(ft(x))p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x)=\delta(f_{t}(x)) and ptplc(⋅∣x)=δ(ut(⋅∣x))p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(\cdot\mid x)=\delta(u_{t}(\cdot\mid x)) converge by continuity, hence ηt​(x)=maxc⁡ptpre​(c∣x)​ptplc​(c∣x)\eta_{t}(x)=\max_{c}p^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}(c\mid x)p^{\mathrm{plc}}_{t}(c\mid x) converges as a continuous mapping. If γt→γ∞\gamma_{t}\to\gamma_{\infty}, then ψt​(x)=γt​ηt​(x)\psi_{t}(x)=\gamma_{t}\eta_{t}(x) converges. ∎

S8.13 Proof of Lemma 8

Proof.

Expand the softmax:

δ​(f~t​(x)−τ3​log⁡π~t)y=exp⁡(f~t​(x)y)​π~t​(y)−τ3∑cexp⁡(f~t​(x)c)​π~t​(c)−τ3.\delta(\tilde{f}_{t}(x)-\tau_{3}\log\tilde{\pi}_{t})_{y}=\frac{\exp(\tilde{f}_{t}(x)_{y})\tilde{\pi}_{t}(y)^{-\tau_{3}}}{\sum_{c}\exp(\tilde{f}_{t}(x)_{c})\tilde{\pi}_{t}(c)^{-\tau_{3}}}.

Divide numerator and denominator by ∑cexp⁡(f~t​(x)c)\sum_{c}\exp(\tilde{f}_{t}(x)_{c}) to obtain the stated probability form. ∎

S8.14 Proof of Lemma 9

Proof.

For any yy,

|rt​(y∣x;π~t)−rt​(y∣x;πu)|=τ3|log⁡π~t​(y)−log⁡πu​(y)|≤τ3​‖log⁡π~t−log⁡πu‖∞.|r_{t}(y\mid x;\tilde{\pi}_{t})-r_{t}(y\mid x;\pi_{u})|=\tau_{3}|\log\tilde{\pi}_{t}(y)-\log\pi_{u}(y)|\leq\tau_{3}\|\log\tilde{\pi}_{t}-\log\pi_{u}\|_{\infty}.
